title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & benchmarking (team wiki)
author: Morgan Lee
content:
Summary

This team wiki consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel-scheduling strategy, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. The goal is to provide a single reference for engineers and SREs responsible for maintaining low-latency, high-throughput LLM inference across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

1) High-level architecture overview

Intro: The runtime is a multi-process GPU-optimized inference engine with a control plane for routing and orchestration. Key components:
- Frontend API proxy: validates requests, enforces quotas, and routes to the runtime cluster.
- Router service: policy-driven routing (latency/cost/region/tier), fallback to model variants.
- Serving nodes: GPU workers running the inference engine (process-level isolation, pinned memory regions).
- KV cache layer: distributed prefix cache for attention key/value reuse.
- Scheduler & batching: per-node scheduler that dynamically forms micro-batches to meet latency SLOs.
- Telemetry pipeline: traces, per-token latency histograms, GPU utilization, and per-model telemetry.

Ownership: serving-runtime team + eng-sre on-call. See "Runbooks" for escalation and contact info.

2) Kernel scheduling strategy (design rationale)

Objective: maximize throughput while meeting 95th/99th percentile latency SLOs for interactive workloads. Constraints: GPU memory fragmentation, variable sequence lengths, KV cache locality, and heterogeneous hardware.

Core principles:
- Sequence-aware scheduling: group requests by expected output length and prompt length distribution to reduce wasted compute.
- Fusion-friendly kernels: prefer fused attention kernels for short/medium sequences where they reduce kernel launch overhead.
- KV locality scheduling: prefer reusing warmed KV caches by routing requests from same tenant/model to nodes with cached state when possible.
- Backpressure & admission control: maintain a small work queue and reject or reroute requests when tail-latency risk exceeds thresholds.

Implementation details:
- Three-tier scheduler: micro-batcher (per-GPU), macro-scheduler (per-node), and cluster router (policy enforcement).
- Micro-batcher window: default 2ms; configurable via runtime.flag.micro_batch_window_ms.
- Kernel selection rules:
  - if seq_len <= 512 and model.quantized != true -> use fused-attn-v2 kernel
  - if seq_len > 4096 -> use chunked-attn with overlap=64 to reduce memory spikes
  - for quantized int8 models on Ampere+ GPUs -> use quantized-optimized matmul fallback path

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile a performance regression)

Short intro: Use this checklist when investigating regressions in throughput or tail latency. Prefer to reproduce in staging with representative traffic.

Step-by-step procedure:
1. Validate the symptom: collect 1h of perf traces and compare p50/p95/p99 for tokens/sec and request latency.
2. Check recent releases: map timestamps to deployments using release tags and rollout IDs.
3. Run perf collection:
   - enable flame graphs: runtime admin CLI `rictl profile start --duration 120s --flamegraph`
   - capture GPU metrics: nvidia-smi dmon + DCGM telemetry for 120s
   - capture kernel traces: `TRACE=kernel` environment on staging nodes (limited to 3 nodes)
4. Correlate with scheduler events: collect micro-batch sizes and kernel selection logs (`/var/log/serving/scheduler.log`) for the window.
5. Analyze KV cache hit ratios: query cache dashboard and `rictl cache-stats` for hot keys.
6. Run focused benchmarks: isolated perf harness (see Benchmarking suite).
7. Mitigation: roll back kernel selector or adjust micro-batch window and sched thresholds, then redeploy canary and monitor.

Common signals and interpretation:
- Rising kernel launch overhead and low GPU SM utilization -> likely suboptimal kernel choice (switch to fused kernel).
- High device memory spikes aligned with long sequences -> enable chunked attention or increase overlap to avoid OOMs.
- Degraded tail latency with small batch sizes -> reduce micro_batch_window_ms and enable adaptive batching.

4) Benchmarking suite (how-to, scenarios, and configs)

Purpose: provide reproducible benchmarks for model variants, quantization profiles, and kernel builds across representative workloads.

Benchmark environments:
- Core lab: A100-80GB (shared), Ampere-48GB (dedicated hosts), and AMD MI250 test nodes.
- CI-perf: smoke benchmarks running on smallest GPU (T4-equivalent) for regressions.

Representative workloads:
- Chat interactive: 32 concurrent sessions, prompt median 64 tokens, gen length 128 tokens.
- Embeddings batch: 1024 batched requests of 512-dim inputs.
- Long-context reasoning: seq_len 8192 steps, gen length 512, KV cache stress.

Benchmark config table:
| scenario | nodes | seq_len | concurrency | micro_batch_window_ms | kernel_flags | notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| chat-interactive | 1 GPU | 512 | 32 | 2 | fused-attn-v2 | baseline for p95 latency |
| embeddings-batch | 1 GPU | 256 | 1024 | 5 | batched-matmul | measures throughput |
| long-context | 2 GPUs | 8192 | 8 | 1 | chunked-attn overlap=64 | memory stress test |

Running a benchmark (example):
- Checkout perf-harness: `git clone git@repo:redwood/perf-harness.git && cd perf-harness`
- Launch lab job: `ri-lab submit --image perf:v2 --nodes a100:1 --config configs/chat-benchmark.yaml`
- Collect results: `rictl bench results --job-id <id> --format json > results.json`
- Compare with baseline: `bench-compare baseline.json results.json --metrics p50 p95 p99 tokens_per_sec`

Baseline expectations (chat-interactive on A100-80GB): p50 < 40ms, p95 < 120ms, p99 < 220ms for the standard gpt-like family at 512 context.

5) Release notes (recent changes relevant to runtime)

2026-12-15 (v2026.12.15-runtime):
- Improved kernel selector: lower kernel-launch overhead for short sequences by ~12% p95.
- Adaptive micro-batching enabled in staging by default.
- Fixed regression causing elevated CPU-side serialization during kernel fallback paths.

2026-10-02 (v2026.10.02-runtime):
- Added chunked-attention path for sequences >4096 with configurable overlap.
- Exposed `runtime.flag.kv_cache_prefer_local` for routing hints.

6) Known issues (operational, prioritized)

P1: Intermittent p99 spikes on Ampere-48GB when mixed precision kernels fall back to FP32.
- Symptoms: 99th percentile latency spikes for short-sequence workloads.
- Workaround: pin workloads to fused-attn-v2 via per-model config: `model.config.kernel_preference: fused-attn-v2` until hotfix rollouts.

P2: KV cache invalidation race during model rollout with canary traffic.
- Symptoms: increased cold-start latency for a subset of requests for ~30s after rollout.
- Workaround: schedule KV warmup job post-rollout and pause aggressive autoscaling for 60s.

P3: Occasional OOMs on long-context tests with overlap misconfiguration.
- Symptoms: OOM traces and abrupt process restarts.
- Workaround: set `chunked_attn_overlap` to 32 and retry helm rollout.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

A. Tail latency spike immediate response (SRE runbook)
1. Confirm spike: query dashboard p95/p99 and correlate with deploy timestamps.
2. Identify affected model(s): filter telemetry by model_id and node pool.
3. Collect traces: use `rictl trace collect --window 120s --nodes <node-ids>` and store artifacts in Jira ticket.
4. Rapid mitigations:
   - Switch kernel selector: `rictl config set runtime.kernel_selector.model.<model_id> fused-attn-v2`
   - Reduce micro_batch_window: `rictl config set runtime.micro_batch_window_ms 1` for canary nodes
5. If mitigations restore SLOs, schedule a controlled rollout of the config change and root-cause analysis.

B. OOM on long-context job
1. Check pod logs and dmesg for OOM killer messages.
2. If OOM caused by GPU memory fragmentation, restart the process on a clean node.
3. Apply chunked-attn path and reduce overlap.
4. Run post-fix benchmark and monitor memory metrics for 10m.

8) Team wiki & knowledge transfer

- Add new kernel builds to the kernel-build index page with measured perf deltas.
- When onboarding, run the onboarding perf checklist: run chat-interactive and long-context benchmarks and post results to #serving-runtime on Slack.
- For architecture changes, create an ADR and link it to the relevant code PR and this wiki page.

Appendix A: example configs (YAML)
```yaml
runtime:
  micro_batch_window_ms: 2
  kernel_selector:
    default: fused-attn-v2
    overrides:
      - model_id: "llama-extended-8k"
        selector: chunked-attn
  kv_cache:
    prefer_local: true
    ttl_seconds: 3600
```

Appendix B: helpful CLI snippets
- Start profiling: `rictl profile start --duration 120s --flamegraph --out /tmp/trace.svg`
- Get micro-batch stats: `rictl metrics tail --filter scheduler.batch_size --window 60s`
- Force canary rollback: `rictl rollout rollback --deployment <id> --to-revision <rev>`

Appendix C: ownership and contacts
- Owners: serving-runtime team (on-call rotation in PagerDuty: PGID: SRV-CORE)
- Primary contacts: Morgan Lee (author), Aisha Patel (tech lead), Carlos Mendez (SRE)
- Slack: #serving-runtime, #serving-runtime-oncall
